newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts await key Thailand central bank data.
newsitem.headline: Analysts await key Thailand central bank data.

text.p: Analysts expect to get a better idea about Thailand's depressed exports picture and see if a rise in investment and manufacturing has been sustained when the central bank releases key indicators on Thursday.

The consensus among analysts on Tuesday was that November exports, the latest monthly data to become available, should improve over the previous month but that year-on-year growth would remain extremely poor.
The Bank of Thailand will release trade and current account deficit data for November, and December data for other major indicators.

"Trade figures will continue to be the focus. We expect the trade deficit for November to narrow due to better performance of exports and slower imports," said Arporn Chewakrengkrai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Arporn forecast that November exports would rise to 120-125 billion baht ($4.8-5.0 billion) from 116.4 billion baht ($4.7 billion) in October. She attributed the projected increase to a recovery in the US economy.
The November trade deficit should narrow to around 25 billion baht from 36.2 billion in October, she said.

"Imports should ease from 152.6 billion last month due to a decrease in raw material imports. Moreover, the import figure in October was high, partly because of the purchase of an aircraft," she added.
But Lehman Brothers' Paul Alapat said any rise in exports was unlikely to be substantial enough to avert a situation where exports growth in 1996 would be the lowest for decades.
Alapat said Lehman Brothers' projection for 1996 export growth was 0.5 percent, the lowest in decades. Thailand posted a 1995 export growth of 23.6 percent.
Lehman Brothers' projection was still more optimistic than that of the BOT, which forecast a contraction of 0.1 percent.
Other economists said they would watch the investment index and manufacturing production data.

"Anything month-on-month that I would look at would be investment and manufacturing production, which have shown improvement since August," Alapat said. "We want to see if the improvement was sustained."
Thailand's current account deficit, which was until recently an attention-grabber, would not take centre-stage because most analysts did not anticipate any drastic change.
"Actually, it could even narrow further from October on the back of an improved service account," said Kanchit Assavasamran, an economist at Vickers Ballas.
Thailand's high season for tourism started in about November. Kanchit based his forecast on the assumption that the revenue from tourism had increased.
The BOT has projected the 1996 current account deficit at 8.2 percent of gross domestic product.
